manuscript.title: An effective gbest-guided gravitational search algorithm for real-parameter optimization and its application in training of feedforward neural networks
manuscript.abstract_text: Gravitational search algorithm (GSA) is a recently introduced meta-heuristic that has shown great per- formance in numerical function optimization and solving real world problems. GSA provides an excellent social interaction between its search agents. This social interaction results in admirable exploration of the search space and gives a unique social component to GSA. However, the social interaction is not able to exploit good solutions in an eﬃcient manner. To overcome this problem, a novel algorithm named as gbest-guided gravitational search algorithm (GG-GSA) has been proposed by utilizing the global best (gbest) solution in the force calculation equation of GSA. The employment of gbest solution in any op- timization algorithm is a tough task and can lead to premature convergence. In the proposed algorithm, the gbest solution is used adaptively and is able to achieve a better trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The performance of the proposed algorithm is compared with GSA and its variants on dif- ferent suites of well-known benchmark test functions. The experimental results show that the GG-GSA performs better than other algorithms for most of the benchmark test functions. Furthermore, to test the ability of the proposed algorithm in solving real world applications, training of feedforward neural net- work problem is chosen. The results demonstrated the exceptional performance of GG-GSA on real world data-set.

sections.body_text: In the last three decades nature inspired algorithms have been widely investigated and applied to various real-world optimization problems, e.g., image processing [1,2] , data clustering [3] , neural network training [4,5] , graph theory [6] , economic dispatch [7] , etc. Among the class of nature inspired algorithms, the gravitational search algorithm (GSA) is a novel meta-heuristic search algorithm proposed by Rashedi et al. [8] . This physics based algorithm is in- spired by the Newtons’s law of gravity and motion. In GSA, the search entities are group of masses (search agents) which com- municate with each other on the basis of Newtonian gravity and laws of the motion. In GSA, there are three main calculations, i.e., gravitational force calculation between different agents, accelera- tion calculation and velocity calculation of each agent. In gravita- tional force calculation, an agent tries to search for global optimum by learning from K best selected agents. K best is a linearly decreas- ∗Corresponding author. Initially, the learning from K best agents results in the good exploration of the search space but with the lapse of time only fewer agents are se- lected for learning which results in exploitation of good solutions. In this way GSA is able to provide a good trade-off between explo- ration and exploitation. However, some researchers try to enhance the performance of GSA by ﬁnding different ways for balancing exploration and ex- ploitation. One common trend is to hybridize GSA with other ex- isting metaheuristics. Mirjalili and Hashim [9] introduced a hybrid approach by combining particle swarm optimization and gravita- tional search algorithm (PSOGSA). In PSOGSA, the social thinking of PSO is embedded into GSA. Li et al. [10] proposed a combination of differential evolutionary algorithm and gravitational search algo- rithm for unconstrained optimization problems. For image segmen- tation, a novel hybrid genetic algorithm based gravitational search algorithm was proposed by Sun and Zhang [11] . Jayaprakasam et al. [12] proposed PSOGSA-E by adding the cognitive compo- nent of PSO to PSOGSA algorithm and claimed that their proposed algorithm can better deal with premature convergence problem. The corresponding velocity of agent i is defined as: V i = v 1 i , . . . , v n i , . . . , v dim i (9) The position of all agents is checked for boundary constraints. If any agent’s position is out of the problem search space than the agent is discarded and randomly, another agent is generated within the given boundaries of the search space. The ﬁtness evaluation of current population of agents per- formed through considered objective function followed by the cal- culation of masses of all agents as shown below: m i (t ) = f it ness i (t ) −worst (t ) best (t ) −worst (t ) , i = 1 , 2 , 3 , . . . . . . .N (10) M i (t) = m i (t) � N j=1 m j (t) . (11) where M i ( t ) is the gravitational mass of agent i at iteration t . Fit- ness of an agent i at iteration t is represented by ﬁtness i ( t ). The best ( t ) and worst ( t ) represents the best and worst agent of the it- eration t in terms of ﬁtness value. For a minimization problem the best ( t ) and worst ( t ) are deﬁned in Eqs. (12) and (13) as follows: best (t ) = min jε{ 1 , ... .,N} f it ness j (t ) , (12) worst (t ) = max jε{ 1 , ... .,N} f it ness j (t ) . (13) In GSA, the mass calculation is a user deﬁned function; hence, one can come up with his/her own function for mass calculation. The condition is that the agent with the best ﬁtness must have the highest mass while the worst has the least. The mass of an agent plays a crucial role in generating the force of attraction. All the agents try to attract each other with a gravitational force which is directly proportional to the product of their masses. An agent i attracts every other agent j in dth dimension with a force deﬁned in Eq. (14) , F d ij (t) = G (t ) M i (t ) × M j (t) R ij (t ) + ε � x d j (t ) −x d i (t ) � , (14) where M i and M j are the gravitational mass related to agents i and j respectively, ε is a small constant and R ij is the Euclidean distance between the two agents i and j : R ij (t) = ∥ X i (t ) , X j (t ) ∥ 2 , (15) G ( t ) is the value of gravitational constant G , at time t , which can be calculated as follows: G (t) = G 0 × exp � −α × t maxiteration � . (16) where G 0 is the initial value of gravitational constant, α is the co- eﬃcient by which gravitational force will decrease. The t and max- iteration refers to the value of current iteration and the maximum number of iterations respectively. From Eq. (16) , it is clear that G is a function of time and its value decreases with increase in the number of iterations. The reason behind of this reduction is that GSA requires exploration in the early iterations and higher value of G results in more movement of agents which provides exploration.

As mentioned previously, exploration and exploitation are the two most common characteristics of population-based algorithms. To attain the optimal solution, an algorithm must perform these two vital process sensibly. In GSA, initially, the value of the gravitational constant G is high which results in fast movement of search agents. The good pace of the agents explore the search space eﬃciently. To exploit the good solutions in later iterations, the value of gravitational con- stant G is decreases continuously as seen from Eq. (16) . The lower value of G signiﬁcantly degrade the intensity of the attractive force and unfortunately results in slow movement of search agents. The slow movement of search agents negatively effects the convergence speed and increases the chance of local stagnation [14] . The prob- lem of slow movement of agents in later iterations can be seen graphically in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 shows a hypothetical scenario of movement of search agents in GSA. In these scenarios, the three agents having mass M 1 , M 2 and M 3 are endeavoring to reach at global optimal solu- tion. The three search agents are trying to attract each other with a gravitational force that can be calculated by Eq. (14) . It can be observed that at iteration t , mass M 1 is near to the optimal solu- tion and possess more mass as compared to masses M 2 and M 3 . At iteration t + 1 , the three masses move towards the center of mass of other agents in the neighborhood instead of moving to- wards the global optimal solution. The mass M 1 lost his ﬁtness to some extent because of moving opposite to the optimal position whereas, masses M 2 and M 3 are in the right direction. However, due to deﬁciency of suﬃcient intensity of gravitational force, M 2 and M 3 cannot cross the position of M 1 to attain the optimal or near optimal position. This phenomenon happens because of the slow movement of masses (search agents) and results in poor con- vergence. In iteration t + 2 , all the three masses converge in a po- sition which is far from the global optimal solution.

sections.heading_text: Solution of slow movement of agents by GG-GSA
sections.body_text: Basically, the proposed algorithm employs gbest-guidance to enhance the exploitation of good solutions in the later iterations. With the addition of gbest-component, the effective acceleration of the search agents is also increased which helps GG-GSA to deal with the problem of slow movement of agents. In Fig. 4 , the position of agents at iteration t depict the same scenario in which search agents of GSA converge in a sub-optimal position due to the slow movement of agents. While dealing the same situation, GG-GSA agents act differently than GSA. The pro- posed algorithm calculates the gravitational force among search agents using Eq. (21) . The addition of gbest-component and higher values of acceleration coeﬃcients c 1 , c 2 increases the acceleration of search agents in the later iteration as compared to GSA. That high acceleration allows the GG-GSA agents to escape the local stagnation. So, at iteration t + 1 , M 2 cross the position of M 1 as the acceleration caused by intensity of the attracting gravitational force is more. The agent having mass M 3 also comes near the op- timal solution position whereas M 1 moves away from the optimal position. At iteration t + 2 , M 1 cross the position of M 2 and has reached near the global optimal position with M 2 and M 3 also ends close to the optimal position. In this way, high acceleration of search agents avoids the convergence at a sub-optimal position.

sections.heading_text: The comparison of GG-GSA with GSA
sections.body_text: Table 1 shows the parameter settings of GG-GSA and GSA used for comparison on above-mentioned benchmark problems. For GSA, the same values of α and G 0 have been taken as given in [8] . For GG-GSA, the value of α = 30 is selected which is differ- ent from the original GSA. However, the initial value of the gravi- tational constant G 0 is same for both the algorithms. The values of acceleration coeﬃcients c 1 and c 2 are chosen empirically for GG- GSA and their transition while iterations are shown in Fig. 3 . The selected benchmark problem set comprises of 23 minimiza- tion functions which can be divided into three categories; uni- modal functions, multi-modal functions with high dimensions and multi-modal functions with low dimensions. The detailed descrip- tion of the benchmark functions is presented in Table A.17 . The results of benchmark functions are averaged for 30 runs, and the average mean ﬁtness, best-so-far ﬁtness and standard de- viation of the results are presented. The stopping criterion for both the algorithms is the maximum number of function evaluations and its value is set to 50, 0 0 0. The experimental results of GG-GSA and GSA on benchmark functions is shown in Table 2 .

Category I: Unimodal functions . Functions f 1 to f 7 are unimodal functions. From Table 2 , it can be observed that GG-GSA performs better than GSA in 5 unimodal functions. In function f 6 both the algorithms are able to reach global optima while in function f 7 , GG-GSA performance is competitive to GSA. The function f 7 is the Quartic function (noisy), and it’s hard to ﬁnd the optimum solution in presence of noise. Category II: Multi-modal functions with high dimensions . Func- tions f 8 to f 13 are multi-modal functions with high dimensions. These functions provide a tough path for every optimization algo- rithm because they contain large numbers of local optimum. It is expected from every optimization algorithm to escape local optima and converge near global optimum. The performance of GG-GSA is better than GSA in all the multi-modal high dimension functions except function f 12 . Moreover, the performance of the proposed al- gorithm is exceptionally better than GSA in f 10 , f 11 and f 13 . In func- tion f 8 and f 9 , the performance of GG-GSA is better than GSA, but GSA is also showing competitive performance. In function f 12 , the performance of GG-GSA is not good regarding average mean ﬁt- ness, but it can be observed that the best ﬁtness achieved by GG- GSA is far better than GSA, which shows the level of optimization GG-GSA can achieve. Category III: Multi-modal functions with low dimensions . Func- tions f 14 to f 23 are the multi-modal functions with low dimensions. These functions possess a less number of local optimum as com- pared to category II functions but, the robustness of optimization algorithms can be analyzed on these functions. Out of the ten func- tions in this category, in 6 functions the performance of GG-GSA and GSA is at par. In function f 14 , f 15 , f 21 and f 23 , one can see the better results shown by the proposed algorithm which proves that GG-GSA is better than GSA concerning robustness also. In these four functions, GSA is not able to maintain its robustness and mis- erably in few runs it deviates from global optima.

To demonstrate the convergence performance of GG-GSA and GSA, six popular benchmark functions are taken by selecting two representative functions from each category. The six functions here are f 1 (Sphere (UM)), f 3 (Schwefel 1.2 (UM)), f 9 (Rastrigin (MH)), f 10 (Ackley (MH)), f 14 (Kowalik (ML)), and f 20 (Hartmaan’s 6-dimensional function (ML)). Here, UM stands for unimodal func- tion, MH stands for multi-modal high dimensional function, and ML stands for multi-modal low dimensional function. In UM functions, the proposed algorithm is able to better ex- ploit the good solutions and converges faster than GSA. This is the result of better utilization of gbest solution in the proposed algo- rithm. Faster convergence capability of GSA can be graphically seen through Fig. 5 . In MH functions, the convergence performance of the proposed algorithm is better in all cases except in Rastrigin function where GG-GSA is not able to tune itself on parameters given in Table 1 . sections.heading_text: The comparison of GG-GSA with GSA, MGSA, GGSA and LIGSA on CEC 2014 benchmark functions
sections.body_text: In this section, the performance of GG-GSA is investigated on all benchmark functions of the CEC 2014 competition on Single Objec- tive Real Parameter Optimization [39] . The benchmark suite con- tains 4 types of function i.e., unimodal, multi-modal, hybrid and composition function. The summary of the benchmark functions of CEC 2014 is given in Table A.16 (see appendix) and the parameter settings is given in Table 5 . On the test functions, the proposed algorithm is compared with GSA and its recent variants which have used gbest guidance or includes modiﬁcation in the force calculation of GSA. In the ex- periments, both 30 and 50-dimensional problems were consid- ered and the maximum number of function evaluations was set to 30,0 0 0 for every algorithm to ensure the fair comparison. Table 6 present the simulation results on CEC 2014 benchmark functions. Here, the value in bold for “Mean” indicate the algorithm ex- hibiting the best performance among the considered methods for comparison. To ﬁnd the signiﬁcant difference in performance of multiple al- gorithms, Derrac et al. [41] provides several methods. In this study, Friedman test is selected to ﬁnd the signiﬁcant difference in per- formance of considered competitive algorithms followed by post- hoc tests.

sections.body_text: Category A: Unimodal functions . The results of all the CEC 2014 functions are shown in Table 6 . The ﬁrst three functions of CEC 2014 benchmark suite are the unimodal functions. In 30 dimension problems, the proposed algorithm GG-GSA outperformed the other competitive algorithms in function f 101 and f 103 on the considered performance metrics whereas, only in function f 102 , GGSA is able to perform better than the proposed algorithm. In 50 dimension problems, the proposed algorithm stood rank one in optimizing

The benchmark functions from f 104 to f 116 in CEC 2014 benchmark suite are the multi-modal problems which contain many local optima. These functions are also shifted and rotated which makes the ﬁnding of global op- tima more diﬃcult. With the help of these functions local minima avoidance capability of an algorithm can be checked. The result of multi-modal problems can be summarized as follows: • In functions f 105 , f 107 , f 112 –114 almost all the algorithms perform equally in both 30 and 50 dimension problems, while in func- tions f 104 , f 106 , f 108 –109 and f 110 –111 , one can easily observe the difference in performances of algorithms. • In 30 dimension problems, GG-GSA produced best mean accu- racy on 7 multi-modal problems which includes functions f 104 , f 106 , f 110 –111 , f 113 and f 115 –116 . • In 50 dimension problems, GG-GSA produced best mean accu- racy on 8 multi-modal problems which includes functions f 104 , f 106 , f 107 , f 110 –111 , and f 114 –116 . • It is evident from the results of multi-modal functions that in higher dimension problems, the performance of GG-GSA is su- perior than other competitive algorithms.

It should be noted that in hybrid functions the variables are randomly divided into some subcom- ponents and then different basic functions are used for different subcomponents [39] , results in the signiﬁcant downfall of the per- formance of optimization algorithms. The same is evident by re- sults of GSA, MGSA, GGSA, and LIGSA. The performance of GG-GSA still remains competitive as it was in basic functions. It can be eas- ily observed that the quality of the results produced by GG-GSA is very high in hybrid functions f 117 , f 120 , and f 121 . In 30 dimen- sion problems, out of 6 hybrid functions, GG-GSA outperformed other algorithms in 4 functions whereas, in 50-dimensional prob- lems the proposed algorithm produced best mean accuracy on 5 hybrid functions. These results evident that as compare to other al- gorithms GG-GSA is able to handle well the increase in dimension of problems. Moreover, the performance of the proposed algorithm is exceptionally well in the hybrid group of functions.

In the last eight composition benchmark functions, the performance of all algorithms is not up to the mark as it was in previous functions because of the com- plexity of these functions. But, again the high standard of quality of solutions of GG-GSA can be observed in functions f 129 and f 130 in 30 dimension problems as compared to other comparative al- gorithms. Here, GG-GSA ﬁnds best results in 4 out of 8 functions in both 30 and 50 dimension problems. To be speciﬁc, the per- formance of GG-GSA in composition benchmark function is best among the ﬁve algorithms. The performance of the proposed algo- rithm and other competitors can also be measure on the basis of standard deviation and best objective function value.

In this section, the computational eﬃciency of the above ﬁve algorithms has been compared. On the basis of mean computa- tional time consumed by each algorithm for one independent run in solving the benchmark functions of CEC 2014, the algorithms are ranked as GSA < GGSA < MGSA < GG-GSA < LIGSA. The standard GSA spends the least time on all benchmark functions followed by GGSA, MGSA, GG-GSA and LIGSA. GG-GSA takes a lit- tle more time than GSA, GGSA and MGSA because in GG-GSA, gbest solution is utilized in force calculation equation which posses O( n 3 ) complexity whereas in GGSA and MGSA, gbest solution is employed in velocity calculation which takes O( n 2 ) complexity. The computational time of LIGSA is worst among its competitors, the reason behind this phenomenon is that different number of complex calculations are included in it. Except LIGSA, rest of the four competitors only checks for position constraint on solutions whereas, LIGSA checks the velocity constraints and solution dupli- cation constraint also. Among different constraints, to check the availability of duplicate solutions is the most complex with com- putational complexity O( n 3 ) consequently increasing the computa- tional time. With analysis of computational time of all competi- tive algorithms, it is observed that the proposed algorithm takes slightly more computational time than GSA, GGSA and MGSA but also counter it with good optimization performance as evident by results in Tables 6 and 7 .

sections.heading_text: Application of GG-GSA in training of feedforward neural network (multi-layer perceptron)
sections.body_text: In this section, the proposed GG-GSA algorithm is applied to solve the problem of training FNN. First, the design of FNN is dis- cussed along with the representation of search agents and then, the experimental setup is presented along with results and discus- sion.

sections.heading_text: Design of FNN and vector formation of GG-GSA search agents
sections.body_text: While designing the FNN, the main issue is to decide the num- ber of hidden layers and the number of nodes in each layer. As there is no standard method to select these two parameters, the method proposed by [4,43] is followed in which single hidden layer FNN is considered with number of neurons calculated by the formula: 2 × n + 1, where n is the number of input features in the dataset. In application of GG-GSA for training of FNN, each search agent of the proposed approach consist of three parts: ﬁrst part con- tains the set of biases, second part consists the weights linking the input layer nodes to hidden layer and the last part comprise of the weights linking hidden layer nodes to output layer. The for- mation of search agent as a vector is diagrammatically represented in Fig. 6 . In Fig. 6 , there are n number of input nodes, 2 × n + 1 = m number of hidden layer nodes and only one output node. More details about the FNN architecture for the considered datasets can be found in [44] .

The performance of the proposed algorithm for training of FNN is evaluated on 16 standard classiﬁcation datasets which are selected from University of California at Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning repository [45] and DELVE repository [46] . The detail of datasets are presented in Table 10 which includes the number of classes, features, training, and testing instances. From Table 10 , the difference in number of features, training, and testing instances which provide more challenge to the FNN trainers can be easily observed. Gravitational based search algorithms are useful to solve many real life problems therefore, a novel gbest-guided gravitational search algorithm (GG-GSA) is proposed in this work. Here, a com- pletely new deﬁnition of gravitational force calculation is devel- oped by providing gbest-guidance to the existing formulation. The performance of the proposed algorithm is compared with GSA on 23 popular benchmark functions. The results show that GG-GSA outperformed GSA in ﬁnding optimal solutions with better con- vergence speed. Complexity analysis of the proposed algorithm has also performed and it has been found that GG-GSA is having the same complexity like GSA. Furthermore, GG-GSA is also com- pared with GSA and its recent variants GGSA, MGSA, and LIGSA on modern CEC 2014 benchmark function suite, the results of which show that the performance of GG-GSA on whole CEC 2014 bench- mark function suite is best. Finally, it is demonstrated that GG-GSA can be used to solve the problem of training of feedforward neu- ral networks. Experiments were performed on 16 standard clas- siﬁcation problems and it is evident by the results that the pro- posed algorithm is very eﬃcient in training of FNN which is due to the presence of good trade-oﬀ between exploration and ex- ploitation. It has been also observed that results of FNN trained by GG-GSA were much better in datasets having high dimensions. The performance of the proposed algorithm in training of FNN es- tablish its suitability and eﬀectiveness in dealing with real world problems. In future GG-GSA can be applied on constrained optimization and multi-objective problems. To see the effectiveness of the pro- posed algorithm in training of other type of neural networks and multi-class classiﬁcation problems is a good area to explore. By adding some mathematical operator of other heuristics into the GG-GSA like crossover, mutation, chaotic perturbation, etc., is also an area of study to further enhance the performance of GG-GSA.
